page: Amazon Web Services m8i.metal-96xl is a bare-metal, general-purpose server type built on the x86_64 architecture. It provides direct hardware access without a virtualization hypervisor, featuring Intel Xeon 6975P-C processors with 192 physical cores and 384 vCPUs running at up to 3.9 GHz. The hardware architecture incorporates a massive 480 MB L3 cache, 2 MB L2 cache per core, and hardware instruction support including AVX-512, AMX (tile and int8), and Intel cryptographic instructions. The server includes 1536.0 GB of DDR5 memory operating at 7 GHz, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. It comes with a baseline network bandwidth of 100 Gbps, zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses, no local storage, and no discrete GPUs.

Benchmark measurements indicate exceptional multithreaded compute throughput and raw memory bandwidth. The instance achieves top-tier results in stress-ng multi-core testing (417,709.66), PassMark CPU testing (181,043.78), and bzip3 multi-threaded decompression (2,054.03 GB/sec). Extended instruction sets and AMX capabilities contribute to high scores in PassMark CPU extended instructions and encryption benchmarks. In-memory data structures perform strongly, evidenced by top-tier results in Redis SET operations (533.75 million operations/sec) and database operations benchmarks, coupled with an uncached read memory bandwidth exceeding 1,169 GB/sec. Conversely, single-core metrics fall into the average to strong ranges, and sequential LLM text generation remains low due to the absence of dedicated GPU hardware.

Cost efficiency is tied strictly to its dense bare-metal footprint, delivering high consolidation value for parallel execution frameworks that fully saturate 384 threads and direct DDR5 memory channels. However, reliance on network-attached storage requires factoring in latency and throughput across the 100 Gbps network interface, as local instance disks are absent. The platform is well matched for large-scale enterprise databases, intensive software compilation pipelines, multi-tenant container fleets, and CPU-based vector or data analytics workloads.
